context: A knowledge store uses near-duplicate detection on every write operation to prevent storing entries that are semantically equivalent to existing ones. The dedup check computes similarity scores (cosine similarity on embeddings when available, word-overlap ratio as fallback) between the new entry and all existing entries. This works well at small scale but performs an O(n^2) full table scan: every new entry is compared against every existing entry. The store currently has hundreds of entries and is growing steadily. The similarity thresholds (>0.90 for exact match, >0.85 for warning) are well-calibrated and should not change.
question: How should the dedup check be optimized to handle growth without changing the similarity thresholds or detection quality?
expert_answer: Replace the full table scan with index-prefiltered candidate retrieval: use KNN (k-nearest-neighbor) vector search to get the top ~50 candidates when embeddings are available, or FTS5 full-text search to get the top ~50 candidates as fallback. Apply the existing similarity thresholds only to these candidates.
expert_reasoning: The key insight is that the similarity thresholds only need to be applied to entries that are already close -- entries with cosine similarity below 0.85 will never trigger either threshold, so comparing against them is wasted computation. KNN vector search and FTS5 text search both provide index-backed approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval that narrows the comparison set from all entries to approximately 50 candidates in sub-millisecond time. The existing threshold logic runs unchanged on this smaller set, preserving detection quality. This converts O(n) comparisons per write to O(1) index lookup + O(50) comparisons, making the cost independent of total store size. The 50-candidate limit is generous enough to avoid missing true duplicates while bounding computation.
anti_pattern: Deferring optimization with 'it works fine at current scale' or 'optimize later.' The O(n^2) behavior means write latency degrades linearly with store size, and the inflection point from acceptable to annoying is hard to predict. By the time it's noticeable, every write operation is slow and the fix requires the same index work anyway. More importantly, the index-prefiltered approach is not premature optimization -- it's the correct algorithm for the problem, and it's simpler to implement correctly now than to retrofit after the store has grown.
